notes.meaning: The bridegroom praises his bride with warm, tender words, telling her twice how beautiful she is. Her eyes look gentle and pure like doves from behind her veil, and her dark hair ripples like a flock of goats moving down Mount Gilead. In the traditional view, Christ delights in His church and praises the beauty He has given her by His grace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view this passage as an ancient love poem that praises the bride's physical beauty from head to foot, framed by the repeated words about her beauty in verses 1 and 7.

notes.meaning: The groom compares her teeth to a freshly washed flock of sheep that has just been sheared. They are clean, bright white, perfectly matched in pairs, and not one is missing. In Christian teaching, this represents the clean and balanced spiritual health Christ gives to believers as they feed on His word.

Her lips are as lovely and delicate as a scarlet ribbon, and her speech is delightful to hear. Her cheeks behind her veil have a warm, healthy blush, like the cut edge of a pomegranate. Traditionally, this points to speech that honors God and encourages others, combined with a humble heart that reverently blushes before the Lord.

Her neck is compared to David's stone tower, hung round with a thousand shields of mighty warriors. This picture shows an upright, stately posture adorned with fine necklaces. Commentators traditionally saw the neck as a picture of faith, which unites believers to Christ and holds up God's shield of defense against danger.

differ.view: John Gill taught that the church's neck represents ministers, who stand close to Christ the Head and defend the flock with the truth of scripture.

notes.meaning: The groom pictures her breasts as two young fawns grazing peacefully among white lilies. The image speaks of youthful beauty, grace, and loving satisfaction. In the life of the church, commentators often saw this as the twin graces of faith and love, or the comforting nourishment of God's truth.

The groom promises to spend his time on the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense until the cool breeze comes and shadows flee. Traditionally, this fragrant hill points to Mount Moriah, where incense was offered at the temple. It teaches that Christ dwells with His people in worship and prayer until the eternal day arrives.

differ.view: Some Methodists read this as the woman speaking, deciding to leave the royal palace and return to her simple home in the country.

notes.meaning: The groom completes his praise by declaring his bride completely beautiful, without a single defect. In the gospel, this describes how believers are made completely clean and acceptable in God's eyes through Christ's righteousness, which is His perfect moral goodness credited to them. We can rest in the truth that God sees His people as holy and dearly loved.

differ.view: John Gill explained that this verse refers to the believer being completely justified in Christ, even while still growing in personal holiness day by day.

notes.meaning: The groom invites his bride to come away with him from the high northern mountains, far from the dangerous dens of lions and leopards. Traditionally, this is Christ calling His church to leave the attractions and spiritual hazards of the world behind and follow Him safely. Believers find true peace and protection by staying close to the Lord.

The groom addresses her as both his sister and his bride, joining the pure bond of family with the special devotion of marriage. A single glance from her eyes and a single link of her necklace have completely won his heart. Spiritually, this shows how even the smallest look of sincere faith brings great delight to Christ.

The groom expresses how much joy her love brings him, calling it far better than wine and praising her perfume above the finest spices. In the Christian life, this shows that Christ deeply values the affection, obedience, and good works that the Holy Spirit produces in His people.

Her speech is as sweet and nourishing as milk and honey flowing from a honeycomb, and her garments smell like the fragrant forests of Lebanon. This describes words of prayer, thanksgiving, and kindness that comfort others and honor the Lord. A life adorned with Christ's righteousness carries a pleasing influence wherever it goes.

The groom calls his bride a locked garden, an enclosed spring, and a sealed fountain. These words describe her purity and complete faithfulness, kept only for her husband. In the traditional reading, this shows that the church and the believer's heart are set apart for God alone and protected by His care.

differ.view: John Gill emphasized that the enclosed garden pictures the church as God's chosen and redeemed people, completely separated from the world and owned only by Christ.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching has traditionally applied the closed garden and sealed fountain to the Virgin Mary, seeing it as a symbol of her perpetual virginity and sinless purity.

notes.meaning: Her life is pictured as an orchard full of sweet pomegranates and the most precious spices, including henna, nard, saffron, calamus, and cinnamon. These rare and pleasant plants represent the rich variety of spiritual gifts and virtues that grow in the hearts of God's people. True faith produces good fruit that brings honor to the Lord.

The bride is described as a garden spring and a well of living water flowing down from the snows of Mount Lebanon. Though she is reserved for her husband, the fresh water she receives flows outward to bring life and refreshment. Believers receive the living water of the Spirit from Christ and share His goodness with those around them.

The bride calls upon the cool north wind and the warm south wind to blow through her garden so its sweet spices will spread everywhere. She then invites her beloved to enter what she now calls his garden to enjoy its choicest fruits. Spiritually, this is the believer asking the Holy Spirit to stir up every grace, gladly offering all fruit and honor back to Christ.
